Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The map is for the volunteer woodland group and not for public trail directions yet. We started at the old stone bridge at 7:40 because the light was good under the canopy and the ground was still damp from Friday rain. I carried the laminated base map, a compass, a rangefinder, and the small field notebook. The phone battery was at 82 percent when we left the parking pullout, and I turned on the track recording there. The first part of the route follows the creek west for about 400 meters. The water was higher than it looked from the road, and I could hear it before I saw it again.

The first marker is a split red oak beside a patch of ferns. The trunk is about one meter across at chest height, and the east side has a pale scar that should make it easy to identify later. I measured from the oak to the bend in the creek twice, first 58 meters and then 56, so put down approximately 57 rather than pretending it is exact. The canopy there is mostly red oak and sugar maple, with a few hemlocks farther uphill. I saw fresh deer tracks in the mud but no scat and no sign of recent cutting. There was an old blue ribbon tied low on a maple, probably from an earlier survey, but I did not use it as a location marker.

At the creek crossing, we need to show two possible ways through the shallows. The northern stones are stable when the water is low, but the approach is slippery, and one stone moved under my boot. The southern route is longer by perhaps 12 meters and has a firm gravel entry. However, it goes close to a leaning hemlock whose roots have exposed soil on the uphill side. Please mark that tree as a caution point, not as a confirmed hazard. The hemlock is roughly 22 centimeters in diameter, and the lean is toward the creek. I took one photo looking upstream and one looking back toward the bridge. The second photo has my glove in the lower corner, so that one is not useful for the final map.

Section 1: Canopy and understory. The western bench has a fairly even stand of mature oaks, with scattered maple and black birch. The ground layer includes Christmas fern, hay-scented fern, and patches of club moss. I also noticed several young hemlocks in the shaded strip between the bench and the creek. They are knee-high or shorter and should be marked as regeneration rather than a separate grove. No, that sounds too definite. Say “scattered young hemlocks” instead. The brightest patch is near the fallen beech about 60 meters beyond the crossing, and the beech is lying across the slope, not across the route. Its bark is loose on the uphill side, and there are bracket fungi near the base.

The trail line on the old paper map is wrong. After the bench, it continues straight north, but the footpath actually swings northeast around a wet hollow, then turns back north beside a low stone wall. The wall is dry-laid and mostly hidden under moss. It runs for at least 30 meters, but I did not follow it to either end. The path is narrow and has exposed roots for about 20 meters. The tread is still visible, though there are leaves over it in places. I counted three blazes on trees along this section, all faded white paint. The last blaze is on a maple just before the path opens into a small flat clearing. In the notebook, I called that clearing Station 4.

There is a spring on the east edge of the clearing, with water moving through a shallow channel toward the creek. The source itself is under a flat slab, and I could not see how far back it continues, so map the visible channel and mark the source approximate. The water was clear, but I did not drink it. The ground around the outlet is soft for about two meters, and there are skunk cabbage leaves nearby, though no flowers. I saw a salamander under a loose piece of bark beside the channel and put the bark back exactly where it was. I will check the photo before naming the species because the head markings were hard to see in the shade.

For the boundary line, I walked from the clearing toward the old north fence and found three iron pins. Two were visible above the leaf litter, and the third was almost completely covered by soil. The first is beside a large white pine. The second is 41 meters farther east, near a boulder with a split top, and the third is beyond the boulder by the brush line. I used the compass bearing from pin one to pin two as a check, but the phone track drifted under the trees, so the plotted line should be treated as approximate. Do not join the pins with a straight property boundary until the land records are checked. The fence itself is down in two places, and several wire strands remain low in the grass.

Before we left, we compared notes at the stone bridge and found one difference. The group map says the creek bend is south of the old stone wall, but my walk puts it east of the wall based on the compass and the photographs. I may have mixed up the wall on the west bench with a shorter row near the spring, so leave both features on the draft and flag the relationship for another visit. “Marta said, ‘The map should help people notice what is there before they decide where to walk.’” That seems right for this stage. We need to add a north arrow, a scale bar, and the date of the survey, but no public access recommendation yet. The next visit should be after the leaves fall so the wall and the iron pins are easier to see.

Final note: The track recording ended at 8:56, and the full loop measured just under two kilometers. The last section back to the bridge follows the gravel service lane rather than the woodland path. There was one fresh tire mark by the gate, but I could not tell whether it came from a truck or a small tractor. I found no litter except a clear plastic corner from a bag near the pullout and put it in my pack. The notebook pages are numbered in order except page six, where I added the spring sketch later. The sketch has a rough arrow for downhill and a small circle for the slab under the source.
